I'm 61 this year, and I've been farming these 13.1 mu for 40 years. I never went to school — can't read a word — but I know my fields better than any book. Our family has nine people, and some of the younger ones work in factories in the city and send money home. That helps when I need to buy fertilizer or pay the electricity for the pump, but I don't like to ask them for too much. We need to keep some cash in case someone gets sick.

My main land, about 8 mu, is wheat and maize, one after the other. The wheat went in last October, same as always. I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu before planting — that's what I've always done. Now in the spring, when the wheat starts to look a little yellow, I'll spread half a bag of urea on top. My neighbor Li cut back on fertilizer last year to save money, and his wheat was thin and short. I'm not making that mistake. Better to spend a bit more than lose the crop. Water from the well costs more every year, but wheat needs three irrigations: one when it warms up, one when it's growing fast, and one when the grain is filling. I can't skip them.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June — we hire a combine for that — I have to get the maize in the ground fast. There's only a few days. My nephew has a planter, so I'll pay him to plant it. I'll put fertilizer down then, but maybe a bit less than for the wheat, because maize grows fast and the summer rains usually help. I'll water it twice. I hope for about 800 jin per mu of wheat and maybe 900 jin of maize if the weather is good.

I also have about 5 mu of cotton. I plant it in late April. Cotton is a lot of work — picking by hand takes forever — but the price has been okay, and my daughter-in-law helps. For cotton, I use what fertilizer I have left after the wheat, maybe a little less than I used to because everything got expensive. Cotton needs more spraying for bugs than the grain crops. I'll water it twice and pick it from September through October.

I don't try new seeds or new methods — too risky. Last year, another farmer in the village tried a new wheat variety and got less than me. I'll stick to what I know. I'd rather apply a bit too much fertilizer and waste a little money than apply too little and have a bad year. A bad year hurts more than a good year helps.
